research.summary:
Every established marathon system builds the week from named day roles with fixed sizes and fixed neighbours. None spreads the leftover kilometres evenly. rocket's generated week (7.6 easy / 7.6 threshold / 7.6 / 7.6 / 7.6 / 22 long / rest) breaks three rules that all the book plans share. First, the quality day is one of the biggest days of the week, never the smallest. A Pfitzinger lactate-threshold (LT) day is 13-19 km in total, about 15-20% of the week, and Hansons' two midweek sessions are 17-19 km. Second, there is a second-biggest run: Pfitzinger's midweek medium-long run (MLR, 18-24 km, 55-75% of the long run), Hansons' 10-mile marathon-pace tempo, or Daniels' 22 km second quality session. Third, the days around the long run are fixed. In every Pfitzinger week I parsed (18/55, 18/70, 12/70; 31 of 31 non-race weeks) the day after the long run is rest, and the day before it is usually a short recovery run (22 of 33).

I parsed the full day-by-day schedules for Pfitzinger 18/55, 18/70 and 12/70, Hansons Advanced and Higdon Intermediate 2 (a third-party transcription; Higdon checked against halhigdon.com). Computed shares of build-week volume:
- **Pfitzinger 18/70:** MLR 35%, recovery 20%, long 15% plus MP-long 7%, general aerobic 9%, LT 6%, VO2max 5%. Longest day 24-31% of the week; 6 running days.
- **Pfitzinger 18/55:** 4-5 running days; longest day 32-38%.
- **Hansons Advanced:** easy 47%, long 20%, tempo 16.5%, speed/strength 16.5%; long run 20-27% of the week.
- **Higdon Intermediate 2:** longest day 31-44%.

The long-run cap is the clearest disagreement between coaches. Daniels says the lesser of 25% of the week or 150 min. Hansons says 25-30% of the week, at most 16 miles and 3 h. Pfitzinger lets a low-mileage plan reach 38%. Higdon goes to 44%.

On quality count: Daniels uses two quality sessions (2Q), with Q1 on Sunday, Q2 on Wednesday or Thursday, and 2-3 easy days between. Hansons uses three hard sessions (SOS, "something of substance"): Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday, with Wednesday off. Pfitzinger uses one intensity session (LT early, VO2max from about 6 weeks out) plus 1-2 MLRs plus a long run, with the MLR allowed the day after the intensity session. Norwegian singles uses three sub-threshold sessions (20-25% of weekly time) with every easy run under 70% of max heart rate. Canova, for amateurs, runs a special block every 3-4 weeks (two marathon-pace sessions in one day, 30-40 km in total), followed by 5-7 days with no quality work. 80/20 runs 6-7 days, has about 20% moderate or hard work, and steps back every third week.

Taper: Pfitzinger's last three weeks are about 81% / 63% / 40% of peak. The Bosquet 2007 meta-analysis supports an exponential 41-60% cut over two weeks with intensity and frequency unchanged. The athlete's 80 / 60 / 32 km sits almost exactly on Pfitzinger's curve.

**Challenges to the earlier research pass** (prior-design-extract.md):
1. It said the brief misquoted Mujika & Padilla on the taper. The figures it rejected (41-60% volume cut, frequency kept) are real: they come from Bosquet et al. 2007 (MSSE). The brief got the source wrong, not the numbers.
2. Foster's training monotony (daily mean ÷ SD) does not condemn the even spread. Measured on kilometres, rocket's week scores 1.41, below Pfitzinger 18/70 (1.49-1.94) and Hansons (1.92-2.34). What is wrong is where the roles sit, not the variance. Foster's measure uses session effort × duration, which rocket does not compute.
3. Its week-5 "medium-long run as a double, 12 + 8 km" is not an MLR in Pfitzinger's system. There, doubles appear only at 67+ miles a week and only on recovery days.
4. Its zero-threshold 100 km week is more cautious than any system: Pfitzinger's peak weeks keep a 7-mile LT run. That is a defensible risk choice, but it is not coaching consensus.
5. Its 22 km long run in a 60 km week (37%) breaks the Daniels and Hansons caps, though Pfitzinger's 55-mile plan allows it.

**Gap specific to this athlete:** his weekday windows (12 km mornings, 14 km evenings) cannot hold an 18-24 km MLR as one run. rocket must either put the MLR on Saturday (Hansons-style back-to-back with Sunday) or treat a 14 km evening run as the "medium" run.

Caveats: I could not open the books themselves. Pfitzinger heart-rate ranges came from secondary sources that disagree with each other. The Pfitzinger transcription may be an older edition than the 4th: Buena Vida's week 1 differs. Daniels' per-session caps come from secondary summaries that agree with each other. Luke Humphrey's own volume guide puts 3:30-4:00 marathoners at 40-50 miles a week (64-80 km), below the ratified 100 km peak.

gapsForRocket: A day-role enum (rest/cross, recovery, general-aerobic, medium-long, long, long-with-MP, threshold, VO2max, MP tempo, strides, tune-up race, recovery-double) with a size rule per role. Today rocket has only kind=easy/threshold/long, and the remainder is split evenly

Size roles as ratios, not the leftover: long run 24-38% of the week (per-system cap); MLR 55-75% of the long run; LT/VO2 day 15-20% of the week including warm-up and cool-down; recovery 6-11 km. Easy days absorb whatever remains

Neighbour constraints: rest after the long run; recovery (or race) before the long run; never two LT/VO2/race days back to back; an MLR may follow an LT/VO2 day; the race-then-long weekend pattern only in taper weeks

Time-window feasibility: this athlete's weekday single-run maximum is ~14 km (evenings), below the 18-24 km Pfitzinger MLR. rocket must either move the MLR to Saturday (back-to-back with Sunday's long run, Hansons-style) or downgrade it to a 14 km medium run. It must never pass a morning+evening double off as an MLR
Doubles as a role: only on recovery or general-aerobic days, split about 60/40, introduced around 100+ km/week; never split a long run, MLR or quality session

Per-session validators taken from Daniels: T <=10% of weekly km, I <=8%, R <=5%, M <20% and <=110 min, long <= lesser of 25% or 150 min. Each flagged per system, because Pfitzinger and Higdon routinely exceed the long-run cap at low mileage

The quality type should change by phase: Pfitzinger does LT in mid-block and VO2max in the last ~6 weeks; Hansons moves from speed to strength at mid-plan; Canova goes general, then fundamental, then specific. rocket needs a phase field that changes the session library, not only the km

Race-in-week handling: a raced tune-up replaces that week's quality session; a marathon-pace race (like Lincoln inside a 33 km day) is the long-with-MP role; the recovery allowance after a race follows Daniels (1 easy day per 3 km raced) or Pfitzinger (rest the next day)
Race-week template: a short MP dress rehearsal 4 days out (Pfitzinger: 2 mi / 3.2 km at MP), strides twice, rest the day after the weekly long run, and running frequency roughly kept (Bosquet)

Gym and swim sessions as scheduled load that competes with running slots: legs day paired with the hardest running day, one evening lost to the swim. Today these invisibly remove a 14 km evening window

A configurable quality-count policy per system (Pfitzinger 1 intensity + 1-2 MLR; Daniels 2Q; Hansons 3 SOS; Norwegian 3 sub-threshold). rocket's committed maxQualitySessionsPerWeekBuild=1 matches Pfitzinger only
Time-based prescription option (80/20 and Norwegian singles prescribe minutes, not km)

A load-based monotony/strain metric (session effort x duration, per Foster 1998) if monotony is to be used at all. Monotony computed on km cannot tell rocket's even week (1.41) apart from real plans (1.02-2.34)
disagreements: LONG RUN CAP: Daniels says the lesser of 25% of the week or 150 min; Hansons says 25-30% of the week, at most 16 mi and 3 h; Pfitzinger 18/70 runs 24-31% but 18/55 reaches 38%; Higdon Intermediate 2 reaches 44%. At the ratified 60 / 80 / 100 km with 22 / 27 / 33 km long runs (37% / 34% / 33%), the athlete breaks the Daniels and Hansons caps but sits inside Pfitzinger's low-mileage range

QUALITY COUNT: Pfitzinger uses 1 LT/VO2 session plus 1-2 MLRs and a long run; Daniels uses 2 quality sessions; Hansons uses 3 SOS sessions; Norwegian singles uses 3 sub-threshold sessions plus a long run; Higdon Advanced uses 2 speed days plus a pace run plus a long run. rocket's maxQualitySessionsPerWeekBuild=1 matches only Pfitzinger

PRIOR EXTRACT, TAPER CITATION: the extract said the brief misquoted Mujika & Padilla 2003 (41-60% volume cut, frequency maintained). Those exact findings are Bosquet et al. 2007 (MSSE 39(8):1358-65): a 2-week exponential 41-60% volume cut with intensity and frequency unchanged. The brief had the wrong source, not wrong numbers

PRIOR EXTRACT, MONOTONY: it cited Foster 1998 monotony against the even spread. On kilometres, rocket's even week scores 1.41, lower than Pfitzinger 18/70 (1.49-1.94) and Hansons (1.92-2.34). Foster's monotony uses session effort x duration, not km. The real defect is role placement and sizing, not low variance
PRIOR EXTRACT, WEEK 5 MLR AS A DOUBLE (12 + 8 km): in Pfitzinger's system an MLR is one continuous run, and doubles appear only on recovery days at 67+ mi/week. A split 20 km is not an MLR

PRIOR EXTRACT, ZERO THRESHOLD IN THE 100 KM WEEK: every system keeps some intensity at peak (Pfitzinger 18/70 week 11 has 7 mi at LT in its 70 mi peak; Hansons keeps both SOS sessions). The prior choice is more conservative than any coaching system. It is defensible as a risk decision, not as consensus

PRIOR EXTRACT, NO VO2MAX: Pfitzinger adds VO2 intervals in the last 6 weeks and Higdon uses 800s, but Norwegian singles ('no need to do VO2max') and Canova (quality at or below ~110% of MP) support leaving them out. Mixed support

EASY CEILING: Norwegian singles caps easy running at <70% HRmax (141 bpm at 201); Pfitzinger recovery <76% (153); the prior design uses 150 (74.6%). Secondary sources quote conflicting Pfitzinger HR ranges, and the book itself could not be opened
VOLUME FOR GOAL: Luke Humphrey (Hansons) puts a 3:30-4:00 marathon at 40-50 mi/week (64-80 km); the ratified 100 km peak is above that. Pfitzinger 12/70 peaks at 113 km for the same general audience
HANSONS vs PFITZINGER ON THE DAY AFTER THE LONG RUN: Hansons prescribes an easy 6-8 mi Monday (cumulative fatigue); Pfitzinger and Higdon prescribe rest or cross-training

verification.verdictSummary:
The sweep is substantially sound. Every one of the 29 sources exists and says roughly what was claimed; I found no fabricated citations or wrong URLs. The four PubMed abstracts were checked through NCBI E-utilities, since the pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov pages would not load; the two PMC reviews were opened directly. I re-parsed the time-to-run plan files myself, and every Pfitzinger and Hansons template week matches day for day. The key statistics also hold: 18/70 role shares (MLR 35.3%, recovery 20.4%, long 14.5%, MP 7.3%, general aerobic 9.0%, LT 6.4%, VO2 5.1%), longest-day ranges, km monotony, 22/33 recovery before the long run, rest on 48/48 Mondays, and 7 of 12 LT/VO2 sessions followed by an MLR.

Errors to fix:
1. MLR size is 52-94% of the long run, not 55-75%.
2. The LT day is 14-25% of the week, not 15-20%.
3. The first Pfitzinger double is at 66 mi, not 67.
4. Pfitzinger VO2 work starts 6-8 weeks out, not ~6.
5. The 81/63/40 taper is the 12/70 plan; 18/70 is 79/61/40.
6. Humphrey's 3:00-3:30 guide is 40-45 mi, not 45-55; 3:30-4:00 is an average of 40-45 with a peak of 45-50.
7. The Higdon week 13 official total is 55 mi, not 50, so the step-back example becomes 55 to 38.
8. The Pfitzinger recovery ceiling '<76% HRmax' is not on the cited page and is unsourced.
9. Canova regeneration is <80% MP and long runs are 85-90% MP (the research said 80-85% and 90-92%). His top intensity goes above 110% MP.
10. '60-80% of Canova's volume for amateurs' is John Davis's own practice, not Canova's.
11. Norwegian singles is 2-3 sessions, not strictly 3.
12. The sirpoc84 page never names James Copeland.
13. The Daniels 2Q easy split contradicts the source (five runs of 4-5 mi).
14. The Norwegian template's per-day km are invented.

Remaining caveat: the transcriptions are probably a pre-4th edition of Advanced Marathoning (Buena Vida's 4th-edition 18/55 taper and week-2 content differ), so exact Pfitzinger numbers may not match the current book. The structural conclusions do not depend on the exact numbers: fixed day roles, a large quality day, a medium-long run, rest after the long run, and a recovery run before it.

research.summary: SHORT-BLOCK SWEEP. Main finding: published short marathon builds (6, 8, 10 and 12 weeks) look nothing like rocket's even spread. In one important way they also look nothing like the athlete's ratified ladder. (1) Short builds that follow a race start at their LOWEST volume. Pfitzinger's between-marathon schedules (Advanced Marathoning ch.12, read through Buena Vida's reviews) all open at about 21 mi (34 km) over 4 run days. The 6-week plan goes 21/35/51/57 mi, then a 2-week taper. The 8-week plan goes 21/32/41/58/66, then a 3-week taper. The 10-week plan reaches a 68 mi peak in week 7. So the shape is: recover, 2-4 real training weeks, taper. Buena Vida scores that ramp 2/5 on injury prevention and calls it defensible only because the runner held that load about 6 weeks earlier. The athlete's ladder (60/80/100/80/60/32 km) peaks in week 3 from a 19-24 km base, and his lifetime best week is 57 km. That climbs faster than Pfitzinger's steepest schedule, without the recent-load context that excuses Pfitzinger's ramp. (2) Recovery after a HALF is much shorter than after a marathon, and coaches act on that. Hal Higdon's 18-week Intermediate and Advanced plans put a half in week 9 and go straight back to full training. Intermediate 2 has a 14.5 km marathon-pace (MP) run 6 days after the half and a 30.6 km long run 7 days after. Advanced 2 has hill repeats 2 days after, a 45-minute tempo 4 days after, and a 19 mi run 7 days after. The lab data fit that. Jump performance was mostly back by 48 h after a half (Costello 2020). CK and soreness were still raised at 24 h (Wiewelhove 2018, Lippi 2008). Gait was impaired for up to 48 h after damaging running (Markus 2025). Easy running from 48 h after a full marathon did not slow muscle-damage recovery (Martinez-Navarro 2021). A half does less damage than a marathon at the same speed (Del Coso 2017). The 'one easy day per mile raced' rule (13 days for a half) is folklore: no originator could be found. Programmable reading: after a maximal half, 2 days with nothing hard, first light quality at about day 4, a real long run or MP session at day 6-8. The prior design's Wed 16 Sep threshold (4 days post-race) and 22 km long run with MP on day 7 sit inside Higdon's practice. (3) The week layout in every coached plan is uneven and role-based. Pfitzinger 12-week, 55-70 mi/week tier: Mon rest, Tue general-aerobic or medium-long, Wed medium-long or general-aerobic, Thu recovery, Fri threshold or general-aerobic, Sat recovery, Sun long or long-with-MP. As shares of a roughly 93 km week: long about 29%, medium-long about 20%, general-aerobic and threshold days about 16% each, two recovery days about 9% each, one rest day. Higdon uses about 12/19/12/0/12/47% of the running km (excluding the cross-training day). Nike says never put speed and long runs on back-to-back days. None of them spread km evenly. (4) How many long runs, how long, and when. Pfitzinger 6-week: ONE long run, 16-17 mi, 14 days out. 8-week: long runs back to 19-20 mi in week 5. 10-week: 19-20 mi twice, weeks 5 and 7. 12-week 55-70: 20 mi in weeks 7 and 9 (5 and 3 weeks out). Higdon 18-week: last 20-miler in week 15, 3 weeks out. Higdon Senior 8-week: 12/14/12/16/12/20/12 mi alternating, with the 20 two weeks before race week. Runna: 32 km at least once, ideally twice, and shorter plans (under 13 weeks) get fewer long runs. Fokkema 2020 (441 marathoners): a longest run under 25 km went with finishes 13.4 min slower than 30-35 km, with no injury association. The athlete's 33 km on 4 Oct, 20 days out, matches the consensus 3-weeks-out slot. (5) Marathon pace against threshold against VO2max. Pfitzinger's between-marathon plans contain almost no MP work (only a race-week dress rehearsal). They keep VO2max repeats 23 and 19 days out plus a tune-up race 13-15 days out, because the runner carries MP specificity out of a marathon. A runner coming off a HALF does not have that, so the Pfitzinger 12-week template applies instead: MP 8/10/12 mi inside long runs in weeks 1, 3 and 6, and threshold in minutes. Hansons caps midweek MP at 10 mi. The prior design's 21.1 km MP block 20 days out is bigger and later than any template (Pfitzinger's largest MP block is 12 mi, 6 weeks out). (6) Taper. Bosquet 2007 meta-analysis: 2 weeks, volume cut 41-60% exponentially, intensity and frequency kept. Smyth and Lawlor 2021 (158k recreational marathoners): strict 3-week tapers go with the best finish times. The ladder's 80/60/32% of peak matches a strict 3-week taper, and the LDNX 10K 13 days out sits exactly where Pfitzinger puts tune-up races. (7) Apps. Runna allows 6-26 week plans but recommends at least 16 weeks for a marathon (Fast-Track: at least 12), with a 10% weekly cap and a deload every 3-5 weeks. Nike: at least 12 weeks, 5 runs a week. Garmin Coach users report long runs capped around 1.5 h / 24 km. Every app floor is above the athlete's 6 weeks.

gapsForRocket: DAY ROLES, NOT EQUAL SHARES: the placement code must assign each open day a role (rest, recovery, general-aerobic, medium-long, quality, long) and size km from role fractions of the week (for example long about 29%, medium-long about 20%, recovery about 9%). It must not divide leftover km evenly. Every template in this sweep is uneven.

HARD/EASY ADJACENCY: a constraint that a quality day or long run is never followed by another hard day. The day after the long run or quality session is rest or recovery (Nike rule; Pfitzinger Thu/Sat recovery slots).

POST-RACE RECOVERY WINDOW: a race event must block intensity for N days, keyed by race distance and effort. Half raced: about 2 days no quality and day 1 rest or recovery. Marathon: about 2-3 weeks, with a first week around 34 km over 4 run days. Races run at MP inside a long day are treated as the long run, not as a race.

RACE-AWARE WEEKS: a tune-up race replaces that week's quality session. rocket needs to know that the LDNX 10K (13 days out) sits in Pfitzinger's tune-up slot and that Lincoln (4 Oct) is the week's long-with-MP.

DAYS-TO-RACE ANCHORING: key sessions are placed by days before the goal race: final long run about 21 days out, tune-up race 13-15, last hard workout 12-13, MP dress rehearsal in race week. They are not placed by week number alone.
MEDIUM-LONG RUN as a first-class session kind for weeks above about 55 mi (90 km). It is currently absent, so an 80-100 km week has nowhere to put volume except equal easy days.

LONG-RUN SEQUENCE LOGIC: short plans alternate long runs (12/16/20/12/16/12 mi) rather than climbing every week. Short plans carry 1-2 peak long runs. Taper long runs step to about 60% then about 40% of peak.

ENTRY-BASE CHECK: compressed plans assume arrival at first-week volume (Pfitzinger 12-week: arrive at 55 mpw with a 16 mi long run). rocket should flag first-week volume against the trailing 4-week mean. Here 60 km against 19-24 km is about 2.5-3x, far beyond any template's largest step of about 20% (or about 50% when rebuilding to a load held 6 weeks earlier).

ACWR / SPIKE-DAY COUNT as an advisory metric: Toresdahl 2023 found injury odds rising with each day at 7:28-day ratio >= 1.5. rocket's config rejects ACWR as a gate. A day-count advisory would still surface the entry spike.

MP-SPECIFICITY SOURCE: whether the runner carries marathon specificity (a marathon raced within about 10 weeks, which lets MP work be dropped) or not (coming off a half, which needs MP blocks in long runs). This decides between Pfitzinger's between-marathon template and the 12-week template.
CUT ORDER / KEY-SESSION PRIORITY: tag which sessions are protected (long, medium-long, one quality, tune-up) and which easy runs go first when the week is shortened or readiness trips.
TAPER SHAPE relative to peak (for example 80/60/32% here) and long-run fraction per taper week, rather than generic volume.

DOUBLES: no published short plan in this sweep uses doubles below 70 mpw. rocket needs a rule that a double is two easy sessions and never contains quality, and that doubles count as run frequency for the unratified-frequency risk.
disagreements: ENTRY WEEK AFTER THE HALF: the prior design opens at 60 km, 6 run days, with threshold on day 4. Every post-MARATHON short template opens at about 34 km over 4 days. Post-HALF templates (Higdon Intermediate/Advanced week 10) resume full training at once, so the prior design's day-4 threshold is inside expert practice. What no template does is jump to 2.5-3x the runner's recent base in the same week. The risk is the volume, not the quality timing.

PEAK TIMING: the ratified ladder peaks in week 3 of 6 (100 km). Pfitzinger's short plans peak 2-3 weeks before the taper (6-week: week 4; 8-week: week 5). Structurally the ladder matches (peak, then 3-week taper), but it reaches peak with 2 build weeks where Pfitzinger uses 3-4 rebuild weeks. His rebuild is to a load held weeks earlier; the athlete's is to a load never held (lifetime best 57 km).

MP VOLUME AT LINCOLN: the prior design's 21.1 km at MP inside 33 km, 20 days out, exceeds every template. Pfitzinger's biggest MP block is 12 mi (19.3 km), 6 weeks out; Hansons caps MP at 10 mi; Higdon's pace runs top at 10 mi. Treat it as an accepted over-template deviation, beyond the Daniels caps already flagged.

VO2MAX OMISSION: the prior design has no VO2max work. Pfitzinger's short between-marathon plans explicitly keep VO2max repeats at 5K effort 23 and 19 days out and into the taper. The prior design's substitute (the raced 10K) matches Pfitzinger's tune-up slot, but Pfitzinger uses both. This is expert disagreement, not settled.

FINAL REHEARSAL LONG RUN 6 DAYS OUT: the prior design puts 18 km with 8 km at race pace on Sun 18 Oct, 6 days before the marathon. Templates put the last substantial long run 14 days out (Pfitzinger 6-week, Higdon Senior) or step down to about 40% of peak (8 mi) about 6-8 days out, with MP limited to 2 mi (Pfitzinger) or 3x1 min (MOTTIV) in race week. 8 km at MP 6 days out is heavier than any template.

ACWR: the prior design rejects ACWR entirely (Lolli, Impellizzeri, Frandsen 2025). Toresdahl 2023 (n=735 marathon trainees, prospective) found days at ACWR >= 1.5 associated with injury (OR 1.06/day). Evidence conflicts; suggest keeping it as an advisory count, not a gate.

RECOVERY RULE OF THUMB: coach content (TempoFit, Marathon Handbook) suggests 13 days or 3 weeks before quality after a half. Published plans by Higdon and the lab data (CMJ back by 48 h) contradict that. Side with the plans and the lab data.

PLAN LENGTH: every app floor (Runna 12-16 weeks, Nike 12) and McMillan's quick-turnaround caveat (only after a recent marathon, one level lower) say 6 weeks is below the recommended minimum. Higdon says an 8- or 12-week build 'probably suffices' only for experienced runners after recovery. The athlete's block is below all of them.

verification.verdictSummary:
This sweep holds up far better than expected. All 36 cited URLs exist and open. I found none that were made up. Every day-by-day template matched its real plan, apart from a 0.1 km rounding slip (Higdon Senior week 3 is 51.6 km, not 51.5). The Pfitzinger week and volume figures come from Buena Vida's reviews, not the book itself, but they match those reviews exactly.

The paper numbers also checked out: Fokkema 2020, Toresdahl 2023, Bosquet 2007, Smyth and Lawlor 2021, Martinez-Navarro 2021 and Del Coso 2017. The PubMed pages blocked the fetch tool, so I read those abstracts through PubMed's E-utilities service instead.

Errors that need fixing:

1. **The largest MP block claim is wrong.** 'Pfitzinger's largest MP block is 12 mi, 6 weeks out' is only true of his 12-week plan. His 18-week 70-85 mi/wk plan has a 14 mi MP tempo in week 13, about 5 weeks out. The point that 21.1 km at MP 20 days out exceeds every template still stands.

2. **The 'one day per mile' rule has a known originator.** The sweep says no originator could be found. It is Jack Foster, in 'Tale of the Ancient Marathoner', as quoted in Runner's World's 25 Golden Rules. His rule is about days before the next race, not before quality training. Advising against encoding it is still fine.

3. **Soreness after a half is overstated.** Costello 2020 found soreness and fatigue back to baseline by 48 h, not raised at 24-48 h. Wiewelhove's CK range at 24 h is 615-861 U/l, not 645-861, and that study only measured to 24 h. The 48 h gait and CK data (Markus 2025) come from lab downhill running, not a race.

4. **McMillan is misquoted.** His quick-turnaround advice is up to 4 weeks of recovery, then a plan one level lower, and only if the runner is not beaten up. It is not 1-2 weeks.

5. **Nike is misquoted.** The PDF says 'try to avoid' speed and long runs on back-to-back days, not 'never'. Higdon's plans put the pace run the day before the long run anyway.

6. **Pfitzinger's between-marathon plans do include some MP work.** The 12-week multiple-marathon plan has a 9 mi MP run in week 6. The '2 mi dress rehearsal' figure is unverified.

7. **The Runna strength count is not in the guide.** It gives no strength sessions per week, only mobility.

8. **Small unconfirmed or softened points.** The 6-week 2+2+2 phase split, the tune-up race at 13 days and replacing quality, the cut-order guidance, and RunnersConnect's long-run fractions are unconfirmed. The 6-week plan's load was held 'a month earlier', not 6 weeks. The Garmin 24 km figure is second-hand user anecdote.

None of this changes the sweep's main conclusions. Short builds start low and ramp. A half needs much less recovery than a marathon. Weeks should be built from day roles, not equal km. A 3-week taper fits the evidence. The athlete's ramp from a 19-24 km base to 60-100 km is steeper than any template.

research.summary:
This sweep builds a session library that software can encode, and it tests the earlier design file (prior-design-extract.md) against the coaches' own plans and the physiology literature.

1. The complaint is about the week's shape, and a variety score will not fix it. The earlier design cited Foster 1998 on training monotony (mean daily load divided by its standard deviation, with above 2.0 usually read as too high). I computed it on daily kilometres:
- Rocket's criticised week (7.6 x5 / 22 / 0) scores 1.41.
- The earlier design's 6/8/10/8/6/22/0 scores 1.38.
- A real Pfitzinger 18/70 week (0/9/14/5/12/5/18 miles) scores 1.58, worse than the week the athlete rejected.
So a distance-based monotony check would pass the bad week and flag the good one. What real plans have is day ROLES, each with a typical share of the week:
- one long run at 27-34%
- one or two medium-long runs at 19-34%
- one threshold or VO2max day at 14-25%, counting warm-up and cool-down
- short recovery runs at 8-13%
- general aerobic runs filling the rest
Rocket needs a role-based week builder. Tuning how it spreads kilometres will not get there.

2. Dose ranges are fairly consistent across coaches:
- Recovery runs: under 76% of max HR, 6-11 km (Pfitzinger).
- General aerobic runs: 15-25% slower than marathon pace, up to 16 km.
- Medium-long runs: 18-24 km at 74-84% of max HR, 10-20% slower than marathon pace, midweek.
- Long runs: 10-20% slower than marathon pace. Caps are 25-30% of the week or 150 min (Daniels), 75-165 min for elite marathoners (Haugen 2022), 16 miles (Hansons, an outlier), and no run more than 10% longer than the longest run in the past 30 days (Frandsen 2025, observational).
- Marathon-pace long runs: 16-20 miles with 6-12 miles at marathon pace (Pfitzinger, McMillan). McMillan's fast-finish version grows from the last 3-5 miles to the last 9-12 miles by 3-4 weeks out.
- Threshold: at least 20 min at 15K-to-half-marathon pace. Pfitzinger's 4th edition sets it by time and progresses from 20-25 to 35-45 min inside an 18-19 km day. Daniels caps threshold at 10% of weekly distance, at 88-92% of max HR.
- Cruise or threshold intervals: 1-2 min jog recoveries. Elite versions are 10-12 x 1000 m or 6-8 x 1500-2000 m (30-75 min of work).
- VO2max: 3-5 min reps with equal-time jogs, at most 8% of the week (Daniels). Marathon plans use 5 x 1000 m at 5K pace. Pfitzinger's 4th edition moved from 1200 m reps to 1000 m reps.
- Hill sprints: 8-12 s flat out on a 7-10% grade with 2 min or more of recovery. Start at 2-6 reps and add about 2 a week up to about 10, once a week, after an easy run (Hudson, Magness).
- Strides: 4-6 x 20 s or 60-120 m, on a couple of easy days a week, under 1% of total volume.
- Fartlek: the Kenyan 1-min-on/1-min-off format, building from 30 to 50 min.
- Sub-threshold ("Norwegian singles"): 2-3 sessions a week such as 3 x 10 min or 5 x 6 min at 78-82% of max HR. The only sources are practitioner write-ups, and they assume 100-160 km weeks.
- Doubles: Pfitzinger says they are not needed below about 70 miles (113 km) a week. When used, they split easy volume 6 h or more apart and never land before a hard day.
- Shakeout: 20-30 min easy plus 4-6 strides, 18-24 h before the race.

3. Placement rules with some physiological backing:
- Heart-rate recovery after a session (Stanley 2013 review) takes up to 24 h after easy running, 24-48 h after threshold work, and at least 48 h after high-intensity work. That supports at least 48 h between VO2max sessions and at least one easy day between threshold-type sessions.
- Marathon-length efforts cause muscle damage that lasts days. Blood CK (a muscle-damage marker) is back to normal only at about 144 h, and jump power is still down 12% on day 5. That supports several easy days after the 33 km day at Lincoln (4 Oct), which includes 21 km at marathon pace. Canova prescribes 4-5 easy days after big specific sessions.
- Daniels' rule after racing is 1 easy day per 3 km raced. That means 7 easy days after the 12 Sep half.

4. Quality sessions per week:
- Daniels: 2 (his 2Q plans).
- Hansons: 3 hard days ("something of substance"), each separated by easy days.
- Pfitzinger: a threshold or VO2max day plus 1-2 medium-long runs plus the long run. No two hard days back-to-back.
- Elites: 2-3 interval sessions plus a long run.
- Boston runners (observational, n=917): more quality sessions a week went with faster times.
The earlier design's one quality session a week, and zero threshold work in the 100 km week, are more conservative than every published plan. That is defensible for this athlete's ramp from about 20 to 100 km a week, but it should be labelled a risk choice.

5. Progression patterns software can encode:
- lengthen threshold time (20 -> 45 min)
- grow marathon pace inside the long run (3-5 -> 9-12 miles)
- raise pace as a share of marathon pace (Canova 80% -> 87-93% -> 98-103%)
- add hill sprint reps before making them longer
- switch intervals from 5K pace to marathon pace minus 10 s in the second half (Hansons)
- threshold emphasis early and VO2max later (Pfitzinger)
- two recovery weeks per 18 weeks
- taper: cut volume 41-60% over 2 weeks and keep intensity and frequency (Bosquet 2007 meta-analysis)

6. Conflicts with the earlier design:
- Its easy ceiling of 150 bpm (75% of max HR) and recovery ceiling of 138 are stricter than every coach. Pfitzinger's medium-long and long runs sit at 149-169 bpm for a max HR of 201.
- It puts a threshold session 4 days after a maximal half. Daniels would allow none for 7 days.
- Its 60 km week has no medium-long run.

Athlete-specific gap: weekday runs are capped at 14 km. A real 18-24 km medium-long run cannot fit on a weekday, and a double is not a physiological substitute for one.

Honest grading: almost all of the session doses above are expert practice. The only trial or meta-analysis evidence is Seiler 2013 (4 x 8 min intervals beat 4 x 4 and 4 x 16 for VO2max, in cyclists), Barnes 2013 (the most intense hill intervals improved running economy by 2.4%), Paavolainen 1999 (explosive strength and sprint work improved 5K time through economy) and Bosquet 2007 (taper). The rest are observational studies or reviews. Some Daniels caps (marathon pace 110 min versus 90 min / 16 miles) differ between secondary summaries, and the book itself was not opened.

gapsForRocket: Day ROLES (rest, recovery, general-aerobic, medium-long, long, long-with-MP, threshold, VO2max, MP, race, shakeout) with share-of-week bands; the current code has only 'easy/threshold/long' plus an even spread of leftover km
A medium-long run concept (18-24 km, 19-34% of week, midweek) - absent from both rocket and the earlier design's 60 km week

Availability-aware role placement: weekday single-session caps (12 km mornings, 14 km evenings) make a real 18-24 km weekday medium-long run impossible; rocket must either move it to the weekend or say plainly that it can't fit, never quietly swap in a double
Minimum spacing between sessions by intensity (easy <=24 h, threshold 24-48 h, VO2max/race >=48 h), and at least one easy or rest day between a long run and the next quality day
Post-race / post-long-MP recovery: 1 easy day per 3 km raced (Daniels), and 4-5 easy days after 30+ km runs containing long marathon-pace blocks

Session prescriptions as segments with dose ranges and per-session and weekly caps (T <=10%, I <=8%, R <=5%, MP <=20% of the week; long run <=25-30% of the week or 150 min; <=110% of the longest run in the prior 30 days)
A progression state per session type: threshold minutes 20 -> 45, MP km inside the long run 5 -> 16+, hill sprints 4 -> 10 reps then 8 -> 10 s, marathon-pace share rising in Canova-style phases
Add-ons that are not sessions: strides (4-6 x 20 s on 2 easy days) and hill sprints (after an easy run) must attach to easy days without counting as quality
Doubles modelled as a split of easy volume only (at least 5-6 h apart, never before a hard day), plus a flag when a double exists only because availability forced it
Load-weighted monotony (duration x RPE or TRIMP) if variety is checked at all; km-based monotony cannot tell good weeks from bad

Phase-dependent quality counts (Daniels 2, Hansons 3, Pfitzinger threshold + medium-long + long) and drop rules: a tune-up race replaces that week's quality; taper cuts volume 41-60% and keeps intensity and frequency
Interaction with the athlete's gym leg day ('legs on the hardest running day'): rocket must know which day is hardest and keep the next day easy
Pace/HR zone bands per session type grounded in the coaches' ranges (e.g. medium-long and long runs at 74-84% of max HR), not a single easy ceiling
disagreements: EASY HR CEILING: the earlier design caps all easy running at 150 bpm (74.6% of max HR) and recovery at 138 bpm. Pfitzinger's medium-long and long runs sit at 74-84% of max HR (149-169 bpm for max HR 201), general aerobic runs at about 70-81%, recovery runs under 76% (under 153 bpm). Daniels' easy zone reaches 79% (159), and Haugen's zone 2 for long runs is 73-82%. The 150 cap is stricter than every coach and would push medium-long and long runs into recovery intensity. It is a defensible risk choice for this ramp, but it is not what any plan prescribes.

QUALITY DAYS PER WEEK: the earlier design allows 1, plus marathon pace inside the long run. Daniels uses 2 (2Q), Hansons 3 hard days, Pfitzinger a threshold or VO2max day plus 1-2 medium-long runs plus a long run, and elites 2-3 interval sessions. Boston data (observational) links more quality sessions a week with faster times. The earlier design is more conservative than every published method.

THRESHOLD AFTER THE HALF: the earlier design puts a threshold session on Wed 16 Sep, 4 days after a maximal half. Daniels' rule is 1 easy day per 3 km raced, so 7 easy days and no quality before Sat 19 Sep. Stanley 2013 gives 24-48 h for threshold-intensity recovery, which is HR recovery only and does not cover muscle damage.

ZERO THRESHOLD IN THE PEAK WEEK: the earlier design sets no threshold work in the 100 km week. Pfitzinger's 18/70 week 5 (63 mi, about 101 km) keeps a threshold day (5 mi at LT) and a long run with 10 mi at marathon pace. The athlete's Lincoln day (21 km at marathon pace inside 33 km) is a bigger stimulus than that long run, so cutting threshold is consistent with Canova's 4-5 easy days after big specific sessions.

MONOTONY AS JUSTIFICATION: the earlier design cited Foster 1998 to justify varied days. On distance, Foster's monotony gives rocket's criticised week 1.41, the earlier design's 6/8/10/8/6/22/0 1.38, and a real Pfitzinger week 1.58. It does not measure what the athlete objected to. Afonso 2021 also notes the index is dominated by session duration.

LONG RUN CAP: Hansons caps at 16 mi (about 26 km) and 25-30% of the week. Daniels caps at 150 min and 25-30%. Pfitzinger schedules three 20-milers. Canova's specific phase has elites run 30-35 km near marathon pace. Frandsen's 30-day spike rule is the only evidence-based limit, and it is observational.
DANIELS MARATHON-PACE CAP: coachray.nz reports 110 min per session and under 20% of the week. Sweat Elite reports 90 min or 16 mi. The book itself was not opened, so this is unresolved.

SUB-THRESHOLD VOLUME: Norwegian-singles write-ups put 20-25% of weekly volume at sub-threshold, 2-3 sessions a week. Daniels caps threshold at 10% of the week. The Norwegian model assumes 100-160 km weeks and has no trial evidence for recreational marathoners.

DOUBLES: Pfitzinger says doubles are not needed below about 70 mi (113 km) a week, and his 18/70 plan has none. The athlete's 100 km peak uses doubles only because weekday availability forces them. A double is not a physiological substitute for a medium-long run.

HILL SPRINT RISK: Magness says it is almost impossible to get hurt doing them. RunnersConnect warns that increasing volume too rapidly raises injury rates astronomically. Both advise starting with few reps and full recovery.

INTENSITY DISTRIBUTION: Muniz-Pumares 2025 (observational) finds more than 80% of the fastest marathoners pyramidal. Qin 2025 (a randomised trial reported in an ML paper, n=120) claims polarised training gave 30% more improvement. The literature is not settled, consistent with the earlier design's conclusion.

verification.verdictSummary:
The sweep is largely honest. All 34 sources exist and I opened them all. Nearly all of its numbers match the pages, and the monotony figures (1.41 / 1.38 / 1.58) reproduce exactly using the population standard deviation. It has one fabrication and several over-reaches.

Rejected:
- McMillan's fast-finish progression ('last 3-5 mi growing to 9-12 mi by 3-4 weeks out, alternating weekly') does not appear on the cited page. The page only has Rosa's last 4-8 mi, with the last 10 min flat out.

Corrected:
- Stanley 2013 is a narrative review, not a meta-analysis.
- The monotony thresholds of 2.0 and 1.5 come from fellrnr. The Foster 1998 abstract gives no number, and Foster computes the index on session-RPE times duration, not on km.
- Daniels allows 2-3 quality days a week (Sweat Elite), not strictly 2. His long-run cap is 25% or 150 min; the 30% figure was not found.
- The Hansons 25-30% long-run cap and 'elites 2-3 interval sessions' (Haugen says 1-2) were not found.
- Haugen gives easy runs as 40-70 min, not 8-12 km.
- Patrice Douge says 4-5 mi at threshold pace, not 4-7 mi.
- Canova's fast progression on the page is 100-106% of marathon pace in 3 km steps, not 20-40 min at 102-108%.
- For hill sprints: the stride count, the 15 s ceiling and 'maintenance every 2-5 weeks' are unsupported, and Magness recommends a gradual hill rather than a 7-10% grade.

Templates:
- The 18/70 week 5 and 18/55 week 1 match their transcriptions. The 18/70 page may reflect an older edition.
- The Paicer week matches its page but cannot be a real 18/55 week, because it exceeds that plan's 55 mi peak.
- The sweep's own DERIVED athlete week breaks its own bands. The long run is 37% of the week, and the 14 km 'medium-long' is below Pfitzinger's 18-24 km definition of one.

Evidence caveats:
- Seiler 2013 studied cyclists.
- The muscle-damage data come from marathon races, not training runs.
- Stanley covers heart-rate recovery only.
- Seiler 2010's 80% counts sessions, not volume.

The main conclusion stands: a distance-based variety check cannot tell good weeks from bad, and rocket needs a role-based week builder.

research.summary:
Bottom line: the science does not support "spread the leftover km evenly", but it also does not say what the fix is. The strongest evidence controls four things: how much of the week is easy, how many hard sessions there are, how long any one run is compared with recent runs, and the shape of the taper. How easy km are shared out between easy days has almost no trial evidence behind it. That part is coaching practice.

1. Intensity mix (how much is easy vs hard). This question is effectively settled for performance, and the answer is that the choice barely matters. Oliveira 2024, the largest meta-analysis (17 studies, n=437), found polarised training no better for time-trial results than other mixes (SMD -0.01; vs pyramidal -0.07; I2=0%). Polarised only raised VO2peak, mainly in highly trained athletes (SMD 0.46). It did not help trained or developmental athletes (0.08). Rosenblat 2019 (ES -0.66 favouring polarised over threshold) pools just 3 trials scoring 4-5/10 on the PEDro quality scale. Festa 2019 (n=38 recreational runners, 77/3/20 vs 40/50/10 for 8 weeks) found no difference on any measure. Filipas 2022 (n=60 well-trained, 16 weeks) found pyramidal-then-polarised best, but the gains were tiny (about 1.5% on 5 km). Esteve-Lanao 2007 (n=12, 5 months) found 80/12/8 beat 67/25/8 on a 10.4 km race (-157 s vs -121 s). The observational picture is consistent. Elite runners do at least 80% of their volume easy (Seiler 2010; Haugen 2022). Muniz-Pumares 2025 (151,813 marathons) found faster runners run more total volume, and nearly all of the extra is easy running. Absolute time in zones 2 and 3 stayed roughly flat across ability levels, and over 80% of the fastest runners trained pyramidal. Rule for rocket: at least 80% easy by time, quality set in absolute minutes, pyramidal (more threshold/marathon-pace than VO2max work). This is a low-risk default, not a proven optimum.

2. Monotony (Foster 1998). Here the prior research file (prior-design-extract.md) misapplies its own citation. Foster's monotony is the week's mean daily load divided by its standard deviation, with load = session RPE x minutes. Foster 1998 (n=25) links illness to athletes going over their own individual strain thresholds. The commonly quoted "monotony above 2.0" cutoff is not in the 1998 abstract, and I could not trace it to a primary source. I computed it both ways:
- By km: rocket's even 7.6x5/22/0 week scores 1.41, and the prior file's 6/8/10/8/6/22/0 scores 1.38.
- By session-RPE load: 1.10 vs 0.99.
Any week that has a rest day, a long run and one quality session sits near 1.0. Only an all-easy week with no rest day goes past 2 (2.45). So monotony cannot be why the rocket week looks wrong. The real faults are these:
- no hard-easy sequencing around the quality day
- no second endurance stimulus (a medium-long run)
- no link between session placement and availability slots or doubles
Rocket should compute monotony and strain as a diagnostic, not treat them as a target.

3. Hard-easy and session count. Seiler 2010 says about 2 hard sessions a week gives the adaptation without excess stress. Adding 2 interval sessions a week for 4-8 weeks improved well-trained athletes by 2-4%, and more gave no extra gain. This is observational and expert synthesis, not a trial. In Seiler 2007, autonomic recovery after threshold or interval work took about 30 min in highly trained athletes but 90 min or more in merely trained ones. Easy running under the first ventilatory threshold, up to 120 min, barely disturbed it. That is the physiological case for keeping easy days easy. A meta-analysis of 27 studies (Inoue 2022) found athletes perceive coach-planned easy sessions as harder than intended (SMD -0.44 for RPE, -0.54 for session RPE). Hard sessions showed no gap. So easy days need a heart-rate cap. Casado 2022 recommends a hard-day/easy-day pattern, but that is a systematic review of practice, not a trial.

4. Volume and marathon time. Doherty 2020 (85 studies) found all 7 training variables predicted faster marathons (R2 0.38-0.81): weekly km, runs per week, peak week, number of runs of 32 km or more, training pace, longest run and hours per week. I could not access the slopes. Fokkema 2020 (n=441 marathoners) found under 40 km/week added 6.3 min, over 65 km/week saved 14.1 min, and a longest run under 25 km added 13.4 min. None of these variables was linked to injury. Tanda 2011 gives Pm = 17.1 + 140*exp(-0.0053K) + 0.55P (SEE 5.7 s/km, 167-216 min runners), where K is weekly km and P is average training pace in s/km. At K=60-76 and P=6:15/km it predicts 3:42-3:48 for this athlete, faster than his measured durability suggests.

5. Injury. Per-session spikes matter more than weekly ramps. Frandsen 2025 (5,205 runners, 588,071 sessions) found a run more than 10% longer than the longest in the previous 30 days raised overuse injury risk (HRR 1.64 / 1.52 / 2.28 for >10-30% / >30-100% / >100%). Week-to-week change showed no association, and ACWR ran the wrong way. Damsted 2019 (n=261) found a 20-60% weekly increase meant 22.6% more injured runners at day 21, with no difference by day 56. Buist 2008 (RCT, n=532) found the 10% rule prevented nothing. No study sets long run as a % of the week.

6. Doubles. There is no running performance trial. Kjosen Talsnes 2024 (crossover, n=14) found two 3x10-min threshold sessions instead of one 6x10 session gave less heart-rate drift, lower lactate and RPE 6 vs 7. Yeo 2008 found twice-every-second-day training improved muscle markers but gave the same ~10% time-trial gain. Elite runners run 11-14 sessions a week. In Garmin-RUNSAFE, runners going 7 times a week had fewer injuries, which is heavily confounded.

7. Taper. Bosquet 2007 (meta-analysis): 2 weeks, volume cut 41-60%, intensity kept. Smyth & Lawlor 2021 (n=158,117): a strict 3-week taper was 5:32 (2.6%) faster than a relaxed 1-week one. By Smyth's own definition, the athlete's ratified 80/60/32 finish is a 2-week strict taper. The 80 km week is not lower than his baseline of weeks 5-6 before the race (60/80).

gapsForRocket: A per-session internal load model (planned duration x target RPE, or HR-zone TRIMP). Distributing km cannot express hard-easy, and any monotony or strain check needs load, not km.

Hard-easy sequencing constraints: no two quality days in a row; the day after threshold work or the long run is recovery, easy or rest; the gym leg session sits on the hardest running day; at most 2 hard sessions/week, with marathon pace inside the long run counted.

Replace even spreading of remaining km with role-based placement: quality day, medium-long run, recovery day(s), then easy fill. Km scales from each day's role and its availability slot (weekday AM <=12, PM <=14, swim evening, weekend <=45), not from an equal split.
AM/PM doubles as a first-class session split when a day's km exceeds a slot cap. Label them as a load/logistics tool, not a proven performance benefit.
Weekly intensity distribution by TIME in zones, with quality set in absolute minutes (not % of week) so extra volume is added as easy running (>=80% Z1).

Monotony and strain computed from planned load as a diagnostic readout (flag >2.0). Documented as insensitive: rocket's current even week already scores ~1.1, so monotony must not be the only guard against 'made-up looking' weeks.
The per-session spike check (<=110% of 30-day longest) applied to EVERY planned session, including medium-long runs and races, with ratified exceptions listed explicitly.
Long-run sizing from absolute distance targets (>=25 km reached, count of runs >=32 km) and the spike rule, instead of a % of weekly volume (no evidence for a % cap).
Taper classification matching Smyth & Lawlor: a down week is below the weeks 5-6 pre-race baseline. By that definition the ratified 80/60/32 ending is a 2-week strict taper, not 3; surface this.
Run frequency tracked as its own progression variable, separate from km. His recorded maximum is 4 runs/week and the block needs 6-8 sessions.
A detector for easy-day drift: realised HR or pace on easy days vs cap, since athletes run easy sessions harder than planned.
An explicit week-1-to-3 risk window after a large weekly jump (Damsted day-21 effect), since week-to-week ratios themselves are not predictive.
Evidence grade attached to each placement rule in the UI, so coaching conventions (medium-long run, 25-30% long-run cap, 2.0 monotony cutoff) are never shown as science.
disagreements: PRIOR FILE vs FOSTER 1998: the prior research file (prior-design-extract.md) cites Foster's monotony as the reason days should vary. Computed, rocket's even 7.6x5/22/0 week has km-monotony 1.41 vs 1.38 for the prior file's 6/8/10/8/6/22/0; session-RPE monotony is ~1.10 vs ~0.99. Both are far under 2.0. Foster's index does not separate the two weeks. The real case for varied days is hard-easy sequencing and slot logistics, which have only practice and mechanism behind them (Seiler 2007/2010), not an illness or injury trial.
MONOTONY >2.0 CUTOFF: widely quoted as Foster's, but it is not in the 1998 abstract and I could not trace it to a primary source. Treat it as a convention.

POLARISED vs PYRAMIDAL: Rosenblat 2019 (ES -0.66 for POL, 3 low-quality trials) and Stöggl & Sperlich 2014 (VO2peak +11.7%) favour polarised. Oliveira 2024 (17 studies, high-certainty GRADE) finds no time-trial difference, and Festa 2019 finds none in recreational runners. Muniz-Pumares 2025 and Casado 2022 show fast marathoners are pyramidal. Burnley vs Foster (MSSE 2022) argue opposite sides from the same data. Resolution: choose on risk; the performance evidence is null.

SPIKE STUDY AUTHORSHIP: the brief calls it 'Nielsen 2025'; first author is Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, with Nielsen as senior author. The hazard ratios are non-monotonic (small spike 1.64 > moderate 1.52), confirming the prior file's caveat.

TAPER NUMBERS: Bosquet 2007 meta-analysis says 2 weeks with a 41-60% volume cut; Smyth & Lawlor 2021 (recreational, observational) favour a strict 3-week taper. The athlete's ratified plan counts as 2-week strict under Smyth's definition.

DOUBLES: Seiler 2010 argues twice-daily training may give an adaptive advantage (Hansen 2005 muscle markers). Yeo 2008 shows no performance difference, and no running performance trial exists. Kjosen Talsnes 2024 supports doubles only as a lower-strain way to do the same work.

FREQUENCY AND INJURY: Garmin-RUNSAFE shows 7 runs/wk with the lowest injury proportion. The prior file flags the frequency jump as an unratified risk. The cohort data are confounded by healthy-runner selection and do not show that a sudden frequency increase is safe.

TANDA PREDICTION vs MEASURED DURABILITY: Tanda's equation gives 3:42-3:48 at this block's volume, faster than the prior file's durability-based 3:48-3:53 band. Tanda was fit on runners with stable training history, not a 3-4x volume ramp.
FESTA 2019 POPULATION MATCH: the prior file says VO2max 53.2 matches the athlete. That figure is not in the abstract I read; unverified. Also the 29.9 h vs 24.8 h are total 8-week hours, not weekly.

verification.verdictSummary:
Overall the sweep holds up well. Every cited work exists, and most numbers match the primary abstract or full text, which I read through Europe PMC, PMC full-text XML, the Frontiers pages and the Seiler 2010 PDF. The confirmed numbers are: Oliveira 2024 (all SMDs, including 0.08 for trained athletes and -0.07 for polarised vs pyramidal), Esteve-Lanao 2007, Festa 2019, Filipas 2022, Fokkema 2020, Frandsen 2025, Damsted 2019, Nielsen 2014, Buist 2008, Bosquet 2007, Smyth & Lawlor 2021, Seiler 2007, Seiler 2010 (2 hard sessions, 2-4%, Billat 78/4/18), Karp 2007, Barandun 2012, Kjosen Talsnes 2024 (+2.8% / -2.5% HR, session RPE 7 vs 6), Tanda equation and its 3:42-3:48 output, Inoue 2022, Doherty 2020, Muniz-Pumares 2025 (including 'Z2/Z3 time relatively stable'), and the km-based monotony values 1.41 / 1.38 (population SD).

Material errors:
(1) The Kipchoge template is wrong on 4 of 7 days. In Haugen 2022 Table 4, Wed and Fri are 16-21 km AM + 8-12 km PM (about 28.5 km, not 37). Thu is a 30/40 km long run PLUS 8-12 km in the evening (about 45 km, not 35). Tue and Sat both have a PUBLISHED 8-12 km (Tue 8-10 km) evening run that the sweep called 'unspecified'. The day totals sum to 186 km against a published 200-220 km.
(2) Garmin-RUNSAFE (Abrahamson 2025) is misquoted. The risk difference of -47.1 compares 7 runs/wk (24.7%) with the '1 time or less' reference group (71.8%), not with 3 runs/wk (59.9%). The 7-runs group is only n=103. 'Healthy-runner selection' is the sweep's own interpretation.
(3) Seiler 2010's 80/20 is by SESSION COUNT, for athletes training 10-14 times a week (so 2-3 hard sessions). The sweep's '>=80% by TIME' and 'marathon pace inside the long run counts toward the cap' are not in Seiler.
(4) Inoue 2022 measures PERCEIVED exertion, at GRADE very-low certainty. It does not show athletes 'run' easy days harder, so it supports an RPE/HR check but not the 'run harder' wording.
(5) Smyth's strict 2-week taper benefit is 2.14% for men and 3.12% for women, not '~2.1-2.4%'.
(6) The Tanda prediction of 223-229 min sits outside the equation's validated 167-216 min range. That is extrapolation and should be flagged.

Unverifiable:
- the monotony >2.0 cutoff (correctly flagged by the sweep)
- session-RPE monotony values 1.10 / 0.99 / 2.45 (they depend on assumed RPEs)
- Casado 2022 'hard day-easy day' recommendation (abstract silent, page 403)
- Casado 2021 R2>=0.57
- Matos 2020 'dip-then-spike'
- Esteve-Lanao 2026 results (403, as the sweep admitted)
- Rosenblat's LWW URL slug (403; the paper itself is verified via PubMed/Europe PMC)

Internal consistency problems in the prior-design templates, not caught by the sweep:
- the 80 km week's 27 km long run is 23% longer than the previous week's 22 km. That breaks the sweep's own 110%-of-30-day-longest spike rule unless a longer run exists in the trailing 30 days.
- 60 to 80 km is a 33% weekly jump, which falls in the Damsted 20-60% day-21 risk window.

The Festa VO2max 'unverified' disagreement is resolved: the full text gives 52.9 and 53.4 by group (mean about 53.2), so the prior file's figure is plausible.

Prior design 60 km week (14 Sep): UNVERIFIABLE as a published plan (the sweep says it is an internal synthesis). Arithmetic is correct (sums to 60) and km monotony is 1.38. Internal conflict with the sweep's own rules: the 27 km long run is 123% of the prior week's 22 km (and of a 21.1 km half), which breaks the <=110% of 30-day-longest spike rule (Frandsen 2025 small-spike HRR 1.64) unless a longer run exists in the trailing 30 days. The 60 to 80 km jump is +33%, inside the Damsted 20-60% day-21 risk window.

research.summary:
What the apps actually do. None of the adaptive apps I could document build a week by spreading kilometres evenly with no structure. The ones that publish how they work share one architecture. (1) Three nested layers: a season or plan made of phases, each phase with a type and a load level, then weeks, then day roles. Stryd publishes its phases as Foundation 70%, Aerobic 85%, Power 100%, Race-Specific 95%, Taper 65-40%, Recovery 75%. TrainingPeaks' annual plan, built on Friel's method, uses Transition 1-6 wk, Prep 3-4, Base 8-12, Build 6-8, Peak 1-2, Race 1-3, with A/B/C race priorities. Only A races get a taper. (2) A fixed long-run day and a fixed number of runs per week, with the other sessions arranged around them. Runna says outright that the long run follows its own progression, separate from weekly volume. (3) Separate, rule-based responses to each kind of change. The rules differ by app:
- Runna: a missed-workout realignment offer fires after more than 3 missed workouts or a whole week. The options depend on the gap: 1 week, 2+ weeks, or 4+ weeks (restart, rebuild to the race date, or continue with an injury warning). Paces change only through Pace Insights, which needs a clear trend across speed sessions and the user's acceptance. The workout structure is kept, and easy runs stay conversational.
- Stryd: a gap of 0-7 days resumes as normal, 8-14 days restarts the current phase, 15-28 days returns to the Aerobic phase, and 29+ days goes to Recovery or Foundation. If reported effort (RPE) does not match power at the current critical power, Critical Power is flagged.
- Garmin Daily Suggested Workouts and Run Coach: the next session is chosen from acute versus chronic load, recovery time, Training Readiness (sleep and HRV), and the Load Focus balance over 4 weeks (low aerobic, high aerobic, anaerobic). Every change comes with a what / how / why explanation. Its known blind spot: gym work and other unrecorded activity are invisible to the load model, so it suggests sessions that are too hard. That matters here, because the athlete lifts 3 times a week.
- Nike Run Club and Final Surge/McMillan: effectively static calendars that the user shifts by hand.
- HumanGO and McMillan: their public claims of adaptation have no documented rules.

The monotony point in the earlier design is wrong as stated. I computed Foster's monotony (weekly mean ÷ SD of daily km) for the week the athlete complained about (7.6×5 / 22 / 0) and got 1.41. The earlier research's 'varied' week 6/8/10/8/6/22/0 scores 1.38, almost the same. The long run plus a rest day already creates enough variance. Monotony computed on kilometres therefore cannot tell a real marathon week from rocket's even spread. What is wrong with rocket's week is its structure: no medium-long run, no recovery day after the quality session or the long run, no spacing between hard days, and no doubles. Foster 1998 tracked session-RPE load, where a threshold day weighs much more than an easy day of the same distance. If rocket adopts monotony at all, it has to use intensity-weighted load, and it can only ever be a secondary check. The week has to be built from role templates.

Load models. Banister-style CTL/ATL/TSB is what TrainingPeaks and COROS plan with. The guidance: CTL ramp 3-8 points/week (Friel 5-8; TrainingPeaks' marathon article 4-6), recovery weeks 3:1 for athletes under 40, race-day TSB +5 to +25. The parameters are shaky, though. Hellard 2006 found wide confidence intervals and correlated time constants. Busso 2003 shows fatigue grows non-linearly with load. My simulation of his ratified ladder (flat 6.5 TSS/km, 42/7-day constants) gives a CTL ramp of +5.3 / +7.4 / +9.1 per week, so the 100 km week sits at Friel's 'crash' edge. Race-morning TSB comes out around -7 under the earlier research's day plan, because CTL built in a 6-week block is too low for even the taper volumes to fall below it. TSB targets calibrated on season-long builds do not transfer. Thomas, Mujika & Busso 2008 is consistent with this: after a period of overload the model-optimal taper lengthens from 16 to 22 days. Taper meta-analyses agree on direction: cut volume, keep intensity and frequency, over about 2 weeks. They disagree on size (Bosquet 2007 and Wang 2023: 41-60%; Mujika & Padilla 2003: 60-90%).

ACWR (acute:chronic workload ratio) is still built into vendor tools. Firstbeat calls 0.8-1.3 the 'sweet spot'. It is discredited as a causal gate (Impellizzeri 2020; Lolli 2019 on mathematical coupling). The better-supported running-specific guard is a single session longer than 110% of the longest run in the last 30 days (Frandsen 2025). HRV-guided training works in recreational runners when the decisions are made on rolling data a couple of times a week: Kiviniemi 2007; Nuuttila 2022, 10 km time -6.2% vs -2.9%. The pooled performance effect is small, though (Manresa-Rocamora 2021, SMD 0.20). Block periodisation shows small-to-moderate benefits (Mølmen 2019) on low-quality trials, and Kiely 2018 challenges the whole premise of periodisation. Treat phase structure as a planning convention, not proven physiology.

What rocket must model: a season timeline of goal races with priorities and roles, a phase pointer with load level, day-role templates, a ledger of delivered versus planned sessions, CTL/ATL from actual sessions only, trailing longest run and trailing weekly km, when the last hard session was, the current missed-session streak, the pace anchor and its trend status, 7-day readiness means, pain and illness flags, and post-race recovery debt. It also needs explicit replanning ladders for gaps, over-performance, illness, and chaining one block into the next. I found no verified real-plan weeks in this sweep. Templates must come from the coach-plan sweep.

prescriptions.rule: Build the week from day roles in a fixed order: pin the long-run day first, then the key quality day, then recovery days straight after each of them, then fill the remaining volume into a medium-long run and easy days. Never share leftover km out equally. Runna arranges runs around a fixed long-run day, and its long run follows a separate progression.
prescriptions.quantity: long run on the same weekday each week unless a race overrides it
prescriptions.source: Runna Support: Adjusting your running schedule; Understanding the long runs; How Runna builds your plan

prescriptions.rule: Do not use Foster monotony on daily km as the fix or as the test for a varied week: the complained-of 7.6x5/22/0 week scores 1.41 and 6/8/10/8/6/22/0 scores 1.38. If monotony is used, compute it on intensity-weighted load (session RPE x minutes, or TSS) and only as a secondary warning.
prescriptions.quantity: monotony = mean daily load / SD daily load over 7 days; strain = weekly load x monotony
prescriptions.source: Foster 1998 MSSE 30:1164 (PMID 9662690); own computation

prescriptions.rule: Put at least one sub-VT1 (easy or recovery) day between hard sessions. Sessions below the first ventilatory threshold, even long ones, barely delay autonomic recovery, so easy days can run back-to-back. Sessions above VT1 cannot be stacked the same way.
prescriptions.quantity: >=1 easy day between sessions above VT1
prescriptions.source: Seiler, Haugen & Kuffel 2007 MSSE (PMID 17762370)

prescriptions.rule: Give each phase a load multiplier relative to peak, and plan every week as a share of the phase load, not as a flat increment.
prescriptions.quantity: Foundation 70%, Aerobic 85%, Power/build 100%, Race-specific 95%, Taper 65->40%, Recovery 75%
prescriptions.source: Stryd Adaptive Training How To

prescriptions.rule: Respond to how many consecutive days were missed, not to single sessions
prescriptions.quantity: 0-7 d: resume unchanged; 8-14 d: repeat current phase; 15-28 d: drop back to aerobic/base phase; >=29 d: recovery/foundation restart
prescriptions.source: Stryd FAQ: Adaptive Training

prescriptions.rule: Offer realignment, with the user's confirmation, only after more than 3 missed workouts or a whole missed week. For a single missed session, let it be skipped or moved within the week. For gaps of 2+ weeks with a fixed race, rebuild towards the same end date rather than extending.
prescriptions.quantity: >3 missed workouts or 1 week triggers; 2+ wk: rebuild to race date; 4+ wk: restart/rebuild with injury warning if continuing
prescriptions.source: Runna Support: Plan Realignment feature

prescriptions.rule: Change pace targets only on a consistent trend across several quality sessions, never on one run. The user must accept the change. Keep the workout structure and easy-run guidance unchanged. Do not update on sessions affected by weather, terrain, sleep or fuelling.
prescriptions.quantity: trend across multiple eligible sessions; manual changes in 15-30 s race-time steps
prescriptions.source: Runna Support: What are Pace Insights

prescriptions.rule: If reported RPE disagrees with what the current threshold/CP anchor predicts, flag the anchor for re-test instead of silently continuing
prescriptions.quantity: per-run RPE vs expected effort at anchor
prescriptions.source: Stryd FAQ: Adaptive Training; CP Accuracy Flow

prescriptions.rule: Downgrade the day's session type (not the week's plan) when acute load is high relative to chronic, recovery time is still running, or readiness is low. Upgrade only when recovery is complete. Show what / how / why for every change.
prescriptions.quantity: e.g. 60 min scheduled -> 40 min on elevated stress
prescriptions.source: the5krunner on Garmin DSW and adaptive plans; Garmin press release 19 Sep 2024

prescriptions.rule: Track the 4-week split of load into low aerobic / high aerobic / anaerobic and choose the next quality session to fix the largest shortfall against the goal-race profile
prescriptions.quantity: 4-week rolling window
prescriptions.source: Garmin Training Status / Load Focus manual; the5krunner DSW

prescriptions.rule: Warn when the 7-day CTL ramp goes above the sustainable band. Treat more than 8 points/week as crash loading, allowed for one week at most before a recovery week.
prescriptions.quantity: 3-8 CTL/week (TrainingPeaks); 5-8 sustainable, >8 crash, >10 elite only for <=1 week (Friel); 4-6 for marathoners (TrainingPeaks marathon article)
prescriptions.source: TrainingPeaks ramp-rate article; Friel 'The CTL ramp rate'; TrainingPeaks marathon ATP article

prescriptions.rule: Schedule a recovery week after a set number of build weeks, chosen by age and robustness
prescriptions.quantity: 3 build + 1 recovery for athletes under 40; 2 + 1 for over 40 / fragile
prescriptions.source: TrainingPeaks: Comprehensive guide to the ATP; marathon CTL/ATP article

prescriptions.rule: Classify daily form and cap time spent in the high-risk zone
prescriptions.quantity: < -30 high risk (a few days at a time, 2-4 times a season); -10 to -30 optimal training; -10 to +5 grey/recovery; +5 to +25 race freshness (Friel prefers +15 to +25 for A races); > +25 transition
prescriptions.source: Friel 'Managing training using TSB'

prescriptions.rule: Do not gate the taper on reaching positive TSB after a short, steep block from a low base. With his ladder the simulated race-morning TSB is about -7, because CTL stays low. Use the volume-cut taper rules and performance markers instead.
prescriptions.quantity: simulated CTL ramp +5.3/+7.4/+9.1 per week for the 60/80/100 km weeks; race-morning TSB about -7 (6.5 TSS/km, 42/7-day constants)
prescriptions.source: Own simulation; Thomas, Mujika & Busso 2008 J Sports Sci (PMID 18344135)

prescriptions.rule: Cut volume progressively (exponentially), keep intensity, and keep frequency (or cut it by no more than 20%)
prescriptions.quantity: about 2 weeks, volume -41 to -60% (Bosquet 2007; Wang 2023: 8-14 d best, SMD -1.47); Mujika & Padilla 2003: volume up to -60 to -90%, frequency cut no more than 20%, typical gain about 3%
prescriptions.source: Bosquet et al. 2007 MSSE; Wang et al. 2023 PLoS One 18:e0282838; Mujika & Padilla 2003 MSSE (PMID 12840640)

prescriptions.rule: Lengthen the taper when it follows a period of overload
prescriptions.quantity: model-optimal step taper 16.4 d without overload vs 22.4 d after a 28-day +20% overload
prescriptions.source: Thomas, Mujika & Busso 2008 J Sports Sci (PMID 18344135)

prescriptions.rule: Do not use the acute:chronic workload ratio as a gate or target, even though vendor tools (Firstbeat) still show a 0.8-1.3 sweet spot
prescriptions.quantity: none
prescriptions.source: Impellizzeri et al. 2020 IJSPP (PMID 32502973); Lolli et al. 2019 BJSM (PMID 29101104); Hulin 2016 BJSM (origin)

prescriptions.rule: Flag any run longer than 110% of the longest run in the last 30 days
prescriptions.source: Frandsen et al. 2025 BJSM (PMID 40623829)

prescriptions.rule: Cap the weekly km increase with a ceiling that depends on current volume, and progress the long run on its own separate curve
prescriptions.quantity: Nielsen 2014 suggests <30% per week over 2 weeks (HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66, not significant, novices)
prescriptions.source: Runna: How Runna builds your plan; Nielsen et al. 2014 JOSPT (PMID 25155475)

prescriptions.rule: Adjust load (decrease / maintain / increase) about twice a week from rolling nocturnal HRV, perceived recovery and HR-at-speed. Never act on a single morning reading.
prescriptions.quantity: 2 decisions/week; 10 km improvement -6.2% vs -2.9% with a predefined plan; pooled performance SMD 0.20
prescriptions.source: Nuuttila et al. 2022 MSSE (PMID 35975912); Kiviniemi 2007 EJAP (PMID 17849143); Manresa-Rocamora 2021 (PMID 34639599)

prescriptions.rule: Use a drop in performance, not a single biomarker, to separate functional from non-functional overreaching
prescriptions.quantity: none: no single biomarker is valid
prescriptions.source: Meeusen et al. 2013 ECSS/ACSM consensus MSSE

prescriptions.rule: Tag every race A/B/C. Only A races get a peak and taper. B/C races are trained through, and their session replaces that week's quality work.
prescriptions.quantity: A races within 32 weeks of each other
prescriptions.source: TrainingPeaks ATP guide; marathon ATP article

prescriptions.rule: Count gym and other non-running sessions in fatigue state. Garmin's known failure is suggesting hard runs because strength work is invisible to its model.
prescriptions.quantity: 3 gym sessions/week for this athlete
prescriptions.source: the5krunner: Garmin Daily Suggested Workouts

prescriptions.rule: Race plans start 13-16 weeks out. Anything further out runs in maintenance until the plan window opens.
prescriptions.quantity: 13-16 wk ideal; max 24 wk
prescriptions.source: Stryd FAQ: Adaptive Training

gapsForRocket: DAY-ROLE TEMPLATES instead of an even split. The week needs roles (long, medium-long, quality, recovery, easy, easy+strides, double, rest/swim). Place them in order: long-run day first, then quality, then a recovery day after each of those, then medium-long, then fill the rest. The even-spread code has to go; a monotony check alone will not catch the problem (7.6x5/22/0 scores 1.41 vs 1.38 for a 'varied' week).

HARD-DAY SPACING CONSTRAINT: at least one sub-VT1 day between sessions above VT1 (quality, MP long run, race, and possibly legs day in the gym). The day after the long run and after a race is recovery or rest.

STRENGTH SESSIONS AS LOAD. Push/pull/legs sessions, legs placed on the hardest run day, must enter the fatigue state and the spacing rules. Garmin's documented failure mode is that unrecorded gym load leads to suggestions that are too hard.

RACE PRIORITY AND ROLE per race: A (marathon: peak and taper), B/C trained through. Lincoln is a C race run as an MP workout. LDNX 10K is raced and replaces that week's quality session, forcing recovery days after it. The race day overrides the default long-run day for that week.

PHASE POINTER with a load multiplier per phase (base/build/peak/taper/recovery) and a recovery-week counter (3:1 under 40). The ratified ladder should be stored as phase and week targets so replanning can move within it.

DELIVERED-VS-PLANNED LEDGER per day, with a missed-days streak and a replanning ladder: a single miss is moved or skipped within the week; more than 3 misses or a whole week triggers a realignment offer; 8-14 days repeats the phase; 15-28 days drops back to base; 29+ days restarts. With a fixed race date, rebuild to the race rather than extend.

PACE-ANCHOR TREND STATE: per-session status (on target, ahead, too hard, variable, not enough data). Update only on a multi-session trend plus user acceptance; keep workout structure; easy runs are never repaced. Plus an RPE-vs-anchor mismatch flag that prompts a re-test.

LOAD STATE FROM ACTUAL SESSIONS ONLY: CTL/ATL/TSB with intensity-weighted load, a 7-day CTL ramp warning (>8/week), trailing 30-day longest run (the 110% rule), trailing 4-week mean km, and a 4-week intensity split (low aerobic / high aerobic / anaerobic). No ACWR gate.

TAPER GENERATOR: progressive volume cut of 41-60% over about 2 weeks with intensity and frequency kept, lengthened after an overload block. Do not target positive TSB after a short steep block: the simulated race-morning TSB for his plan is about -7.

DAILY MODULATION LAYER, separate from the weekly plan: downgrade the session type or length on low readiness, incomplete recovery, pain or illness, without rewriting the week. Decide on 7-day rolling data about twice a week. Every change comes with a what / how / why explanation.
ILLNESS STATE with a staged return. I could not extract the IOC 2022 staged return-to-sport rules (full text blocked), so rocket needs a sourced protocol before it can encode one.

SEASON CHAINING: after the marathon, a recovery block (Stryd's example Recovery phase is 7 days at 75% load; I found no verified post-marathon rule), then a transition, then the next plan's start window (13-16 weeks before the next A race), with maintenance mode before that window opens.
USER-CONFIRMED, IRREVERSIBLE REALIGNMENT UX (Runna warns that a realignment cannot be undone). Rocket should keep plan versions so a replan can be reverted.
disagreements: CHALLENGE TO THE EARLIER DESIGN: it cited Foster 1998 training monotony as the reason for varied weeks. Computed on daily km, the athlete's complained-of week (7.6x5/22/0) has monotony 1.41 and the earlier design's own 6/8/10/8/6/22/0 has 1.38, so the metric does not tell them apart. Foster measured session-RPE load, not km. The case for varied weeks rests on day roles and hard/easy spacing (Seiler 2007), not on monotony.

CTL RAMP BANDS disagree across TrainingPeaks' own pages and Friel: 3-8/week (TrainingPeaks annual-plan guide), 5-8 sustainable with >8 as crash (Friel; TrainingPeaks ramp article), 4-6 for marathoners (TrainingPeaks marathon article). None cites a trial.

TAPER SIZE: Bosquet 2007 and Wang 2023 meta-analyses say cut volume 41-60% and keep frequency. Mujika & Padilla 2003 say cut volume up to 60-90% and frequency by no more than 20%. Both agree on keeping intensity.

RACE-DAY TSB: Friel prefers +15 to +25 for A races; the same article allows anywhere in +5 to +25. My simulation shows neither is reachable after his 6-week ramp from about 20 km/week without cutting below the low chronic load, so the targets do not transfer.

ACWR: Firstbeat (in Garmin-lineage products) still presents 0.8-1.3 as a sweet spot and >1.5 as danger. Impellizzeri 2020 and Lolli 2019 say there is no causal evidence and the ratio is mathematically coupled.

HRV-GUIDED TRAINING: Kiviniemi 2007 and Nuuttila 2022 show clear benefit in recreational runners. The Manresa-Rocamora 2021 meta-analysis finds only a small, non-significant performance effect (SMD 0.20).
PERIODISATION: Mølmen 2019 finds small-to-moderate benefits for block periodisation, but from weak studies. Kiely 2018 argues the stress-theory foundations of periodisation are outdated.

AUTO-ADAPT vs USER CONSENT: Garmin Run Coach and HumanGO change sessions automatically. Runna never applies pace changes or realignment without explicit acceptance, and warns realignment cannot be undone.
TrainingPeaks says a missed day's zero 'is carried for 42 days'. Under the exponentially weighted CTL it decays gradually; it is not held at full weight. The ATP article overstates this.

UNVERIFIED FROM THE EARLIER RESEARCH: the claim that Frandsen 2025 found the largest ACWR spikes associated with fewer injuries (HRR 0.75). The abstract I opened reports only the single-session spike findings, so I could not confirm it.
