verification.verdictSummary:
No fabricated citations turned up. Every peer-reviewed work exists, with matching PMIDs, journals and years (checked through NCBI esummary), and every app page I opened says roughly what the sweep claims. The sweep's 'URLs' for papers are Europe PMC API search queries, not record pages; I have supplied PubMed record URLs. Checked numbers are accurate: Frandsen HRRs, Nuuttila -6.2/-2.9, Nielsen HR 1.59, Thomas 16.4/22.4 d, Manresa-Rocamora SMD 0.20, Wang 8-14 d / -41 to -60%, Mujika & Padilla 60-90% / 20% / 3%, the Stryd ladder and phase loads, Runna's >3 workouts / 1 week trigger, TrainingPeaks phase lengths, Firstbeat 0.8-1.3. The monotony recomputation reproduces 1.41 vs 1.38.

Errors to fix:
(1) Friel TSB: he does not prefer +15 to +25 for A races. He says it varies by athlete, some at +20 to +25, others at +5 to +10.
(2) CTL crash threshold: no source says >8. Friel says 5-8 for most and >10 for at most a week (elites). TrainingPeaks' pages give 3-8 and 4-6.
(3) Race priority: TrainingPeaks gives A AND B races taper weighting, so 'only A races taper' is wrong. 'B/C replaces the week's quality session' has no source.
(4) Runna realignment: rebuilding to the race date is a user option, not a rule. 'Continue unchanged' is also offered at 2+ weeks.
(5) Runna Pace Insights: weather, terrain, sleep and fuelling are things it 'can't yet account for', not exclusions. Steps are 15-30 s for reverting and 20-30 s recommended.
(6) Frandsen 2025: the abstract does report a negative dose-response for ACWR, contrary to the sweep's disagreement note. HRR 0.75 is still not in the abstract.
(7) Seiler 2007 is a lab study of autonomic recovery, not a trial. The one-easy-day spacing rule is an inference.
(8) Nothing on the Stryd page supports 'maintenance mode before the window'. Garmin choosing sessions from the 4-week Load Focus shortfall was not confirmed.
(9) Nuuttila search URL uses Vesterinen 2016 terms; the citation is right but the link is sloppy.

Could not check: the own CTL/TSB simulation (-7 TSB), which depends on the athlete's ladder; the COROS page; Busso, Plews, Buchheit and Meeusen content; the Issurin half of the periodisation entry; the 'small-to-moderate' wording for Mølmen.

research.summary:
Short version: published plans at this athlete's level never lay a week out as equal filler runs around a long run. Every source I could open varies run length on purpose. Each run has a job (recovery, general aerobic, medium-long, quality, long) and each job has its own typical length.

What real 60/80/100 km weeks look like. The best source is a runner's cell-by-cell copy of Pfitzinger & Douglas's 18-week 55-70 mile plan (Dave Bennett's blog). I checked every week's day totals against the stated weekly total. At 106-113 km a week the shape is: Monday rest; Tuesday quality, 16-19 km including warm-up and cool-down; Wednesday medium-long, 22-24 km; Thursday recovery, 8-10 km; Friday a second medium-long or threshold day, 18-19 km; Saturday recovery, 8 km; Sunday long, 32-35 km. At 85-89 km (week 1 of the 18-week and 12-week 55-70 plans) it is 0 / 13.7 / 18.5 / 8 / 13.7-15.3 / 8 / 22.5-25. At 54-56 km (Pfitzinger's up-to-55 tier) it is only four runs: 13.7 / 13.7-14.5 / 7-9 / 18.5-20. The Hansons Advanced peak week is 12.9 / 19.3 / 0 / 19.3 / 11.3 / 12.9 / 25.7 = 101 km. Hansons caps the long run at 16 miles (25.7 km) and has two hard sessions, Tuesday and Thursday. Higdon Advanced 2 and McMillan's sample plan follow the same idea: two quality days, short easy days, and a long run (Higdon adds a Saturday marathon-pace run the day before it).

Numbers a program can use:
- Longest non-long run divided by shortest: 2.2-3.0 in Pfitzinger, 1.7 in Hansons. Rocket's week is 1.0.
- Medium-long run: 16-22% of the week and 65-75% of that week's long run. It is always one continuous run, in midweek. It appears 1-2 times a week from about 85 km.
- Recovery days: two, sometimes three, per week at 8-10 km. That length stays fixed from 87 km to 113 km weeks. This is why low-volume weeks drop run days instead of shrinking every run.
- Long run share falls as volume rises: 34-36% of a 54-56 km week, 27-28% at 85-89 km, 26-31% at 106-113 km, 25% in Hansons.
- Quality days are long: Pfitzinger threshold days are 13.7-19.3 km in total.
- Run days: 4 up to about 55 miles a week (88 km), 6 in the 55-70 tier, 7 in the 70-85 tier.
- Doubles: in the 55-70 tier only 6 of 18 weeks have one, always a recovery day split 6+4 miles (about 10+6 km), and only in weeks of 66 miles (106 km) or more. The review of Pfitzinger's 70-85 plan says doubles start "once you pass 75 miles" (121 km) and that a second run under 25 minutes is not worth it.
- Placement: rest the day after the long run, recovery the day before it. Quality and medium-long can sit back to back (Tuesday then Wednesday), followed by a recovery day.

Daniels is the exception. His 2Q plans fix two big quality sessions of 13-17 miles (21-27 km) and leave the rest as unscheduled easy running, which can be flat 60-minute days. So equal easy days are not wrong in themselves. They are wrong when nothing else in the week carries the load. Daniels' two sessions are each 25-40% of the week. Rocket's threshold day is 7.6 km, identical to its easy days.

Rocket's week (7.6 / 7.6 threshold / 7.6 / 7.6 / 7.6 / 22 / 0) against those rules:
- No medium-long run.
- A threshold day too short for a warm-up, 20-25 minutes of threshold and a cool-down.
- No recovery days that are shorter than the rest.
- Six runs where published 55 km plans use four or five. The athlete has never run more than four times in a week.
- The long run is 37% of the week, above even the up-to-55 tier.

A coach following Pfitzinger's up-to-55 shape would write something like: Monday 0; Tuesday 10 general aerobic with strides; Wednesday 13-14 threshold day; Thursday 7 recovery; Friday 0 or swim; Saturday 22 long with a marathon-pace finish; Sunday 7-8 recovery. That is five runs with a non-long spread of about 2.0. I derived this from the pattern; no plan prints this exact week.

Challenge to the earlier research file (prior-design-extract.md): it cites Foster 1998 training monotony as the reason. I computed monotony (daily mean divided by standard deviation) on kilometres. Rocket's week scores 1.41, lower (less monotonous) than Pfitzinger's own weeks (1.49-1.79) and far below Pfitzinger's 12-week 70-85 week 2 (2.43). Foster defined load as session RPE times duration and linked it to illness in 25 athletes. A distance-based monotony check would therefore pass rocket's flat week, so it cannot be the rule that fixes it. The fix has to be structural: role slots with length ratios. That earlier file's 100 km week also splits a 21 km medium-long run into a morning and evening double, which no Pfitzinger plan does. His doubles only ever split recovery days.

A constraint rocket must handle: the athlete's weekday caps (12 km mornings, 14 km evenings) are below a Pfitzinger-style medium-long run (18-24 km). Options are to cap the medium-long run at 14 km on a weekday, move it to the weekend, or treat a split as a named compromise.

Population context: Muniz-Pumares et al. 2025 (151,813 marathons on Strava) found a mean of 45.1 km a week. A secondary summary (Runners Connect), not the paper, puts 3:30-4:00 finishers at 50-60 km and 3:00-3:30 at 64-72 km, on 5-6 days. A 100 km peak is Pfitzinger 55-70 territory.

Not verified: I could not open any Reddit or LetsRun thread (bot check and Cloudflare 403) or any posted Runna week, so no runner forum reports or real Runna outputs are included. Runna is covered only by its support pages.

gapsForRocket: Role slots instead of even spreading: each run needs a role (rest / recovery / general-aerobic / medium-long / quality / long / long-with-MP), and each role needs its own length rule. The current code divides leftover km equally across open days, which produces a longest/shortest ratio of 1.0; published plans run 1.7-3.0.
Medium-long run: rocket has no medium-long run at all. It needs one continuous midweek run from ~80 km/week, at 16-22% of the week and 65-75% of that week's long run, never split into a double.

Recovery lengths are fixed, not proportional: recovery runs stay 6-10 km whatever the weekly total. Scaling a Pfitzinger shape down to 60 km would make them ~4 km, so low-volume weeks must drop run days (4-5 runs at <=88 km) instead of shrinking every run.
Run frequency should come from weekly volume, not from how many days are free. This athlete's recorded maximum is 4 runs a week; published 55 km weeks use 4-5.
Quality-day length must include warm-up and cool-down (13.7-19.3 km in Pfitzinger). A 7.6 km threshold day equal to the easy days is not a real session.

Doubles: allow only to split a recovery day or to handle a slot-capacity overflow. Enforce a minimum second-run length (~25 min) and at most one double a week below ~113 km. Never split the medium-long run.

Availability caps versus indivisible sessions: weekday caps (12 km mornings, 14 km evenings) are below a Pfitzinger-size medium-long run (18-24 km). The planner must choose explicitly (cap the medium-long run at 14 km, move it to the weekend, or show a split as a named compromise) rather than splitting silently.

Placement rules: rest the day after the long run, recovery the day before it, quality and medium-long allowed back to back followed by recovery, a Higdon-style Saturday marathon-pace run the day before the long run as an option, and a tune-up race replacing the pre-long-run recovery slot (Pfitzinger races Saturday, then 17-18 mi Sunday).
Long-run share should fall with volume (~35% at 55-60 km, ~27-30% at 85-113 km), not be a fixed share.
If a monotony check is added, compute it from session RPE times duration including intensity, not km. On km it scores rocket's flat week as less monotonous than real Pfitzinger weeks.
The strength schedule (legs on the hardest day) and the one evening swim need slots in the week model; none of the plans studied schedule strength, so rocket must place it.
Down weeks (15-25% load cut every 3rd-4th week, McMillan) do not fit the ratified ladder. They should appear as a surfaced deviation, not be applied silently.
disagreements: Monotony as the rationale (prior-design-extract.md cites Foster 1998): computed on km, rocket's flat week scores 1.41 while real Pfitzinger 55-70 weeks score 1.49-1.79 and Pfitzinger 12/70-85 week 2 scores 2.43. Distance-based monotony does not flag the problem. Foster's measure uses session RPE times duration, and his evidence is illness in 25 athletes, so it cannot justify a day-structure rule.

Splitting a medium-long run into a double (prior extract's 100 km week: 21 km Thursday as 12 am + 9 pm): Pfitzinger's 55-70 plan only ever doubles recovery days (6+4 mi), and the 70-85 review says a second run under 25 min is not worthwhile. Here the split is forced by availability caps, not coaching practice, and should be labelled as a compromise.

Flat easy days: Daniels' final 12-week plan does prescribe equal 60-minute E days, and 2Q leaves easy volume unscheduled. Equal easy days are acceptable when two big quality days (21-35 km each) carry the load, which rocket's 7.6 km threshold day does not.
Hard/easy alternation: Pfitzinger stacks quality Tuesday and medium-long Wednesday back to back, while McMillan and Hansons separate hard days with easy days. Both appear in real plans.
Long-run cap: Hansons caps at 16 mi (25.7 km, 25% of peak week) while Pfitzinger 55-70 reaches 21-22 mi (34-35 km, ~31%). The prior extract's 33 km peak matches Pfitzinger, not Hansons.
Long-run share at low volume: the prior extract's 22 km in a 60 km week (37%) is slightly above even Pfitzinger's up-to-55 tier (34-36% at 54-56 km), and that tier uses 4 runs, not 6.

Population volume figures conflict between secondary summaries: Runners Connect puts 3:30-4:00 finishers at 50-60 km/wk, while 42Cal says sub-4 finishers average ~25 km/wk. Neither was checked against the paper's table; only the abstract's mean (45.1 km/wk) was verified.

Doubles thresholds differ: one Pfitzinger review says doubling isn't needed until ~70 mi/wk, Buena Vida says the 70-85 tier doubles once past 75 mi, and the 12/70-85 plan has an AM recovery double from week 2 at 66.5 mi. Treat ~105-120 km as the zone where doubles begin, not a hard number.

verification.verdictSummary:
This sweep checks out much better than expected. There are no invented sources: 31 of 31 exist, and I opened every one. The core evidence is sound. I downloaded and parsed Dave Bennett's two Pfitzinger spreadsheets, and the four weeks taken from them match cell by cell. So do the Buena Vida Pfitzinger and Daniels weeks, Higdon week 13, McMillan week 6, the Daniels 2Q sessions, the Runna figures, and the Muniz-Pumares and Foster abstracts, which I checked through NCBI because the Europe PMC links the sweep gave returned 502/503. The recomputed ratios, long-run shares and monotony values (1.41 and 2.43) reproduce.

Errors found:
(1) The sweep says the earlier research file, prior-design-extract.md, cites Foster 1998 training monotony. It does not; the only 'monoton' in the file is 'NON-MONOTONIC'. The rebuttal attacks a claim that was never made. The split doubles it criticises do exist, but the split medium-long run is the 20 km Wednesday (12+8), not the 21 km Thursday.
(2) 'Doubles only in weeks >= 66 mi' is false. The 2-weeks-to-go taper week (55-57 mi) also has a 6+4 recovery double.
(3) 'Medium-long run = 65-75% of the long run' is too tight. The spreadsheet ranges from about 52% to 83%.
(4) 42Cal says sub-4 finishers run ~25 miles a week, not 25 km. The 'conflicting secondary figures' are mostly a unit error.
(5) The Hansons peak week's Tuesday is threshold, not VO2max. The source states 62 mi, while the days sum to 63.
(6) 12/70-85 week 2 sums to 66.0 mi, not 66.5. A lone Monday AM recovery run is not a double.
(7) 'Four run days up to 55 mi' should be 4-5. Buena Vida and therunningboffin both describe 5 runs a week.
(8) The fast-finish long runs in McMillan's plan fall 6, 4 and 2 weeks out, not '8-10 weeks out'.
(9) The Berlin plan is Pfitzinger's 12-week 55-70, not a '12/70' tier.
(10) Buena Vida lists the 18-week up-to-55 week 1 as bare distances. The sweep's range text ('20-25 min @ LT', 'GA 8-10', 'Recovery 4-5') was not on the page and may be invented.

I could not check the rocket-side numbers (the 7.6 km days, the 12/14 km availability caps, the 4-run maximum) against rocket code; they come from the sweep's own reading of the project. The structural conclusion survives verification: build the week from run roles with their own length rules, recovery runs of fixed length, run days set by weekly volume, and doubles only on recovery days.
